title: Cedaredge Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Cedaredge wells have a 110 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $11,500-$20,200.
h1: Cedaredge, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
This page summarizes Colorado Division of Water Resources permit records for wells within 5 miles of Cedaredge in Delta County. The records show 822 permitted wells, although only 469 are recorded as constructed, 494 report a total depth, 181 report a pump yield, and 27 report a static water level.

For a buyer, the local pattern is generally favorable: the median completed depth is 110 feet and the median reported yield is 15 gallons per minute. Those figures are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee what a particular lot will produce. Ground conditions, well location, construction, and the permit's allowed use still matter.

sections.heading: Cedaredge well depths: mostly shallow, but not uniform
sections.html:
Recorded wells near Cedaredge have a median depth of 110 feet. The middle half runs from 71 to 167 feet, so a driller's estimate around this range is more representative than using the deepest record. The 90th percentile is 229 feet, and the deepest well in the records reaches 800 feet.

Depth mix also gives useful bidding context: 41% of wells are under 100 feet, 56% fall between 100 and 300 feet, and 2% are between 300 and 600 feet. No recorded wells are in the 600-plus-foot category. The named geology is dominated by unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer records, with 801 wells, so conditions can still change quickly from one parcel to the next.

sections.heading: What Cedaredge wells produce
sections.html:
The median reported pump yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 59% producing more than 15 gallons per minute, 33% between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 9% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute.

That is a strong local production pattern, but a pump yield is not the same as a guaranteed household supply. Ask for the well construction report and the pumping information, then compare nearby wells on the same side of Cedaredge, Orchard City, or another nearby area. A domestic permit may also limit how the water can be used. Colorado's exempt household-use wells generally have a 35 gpm pumping limit.

sections.heading: Cedaredge water levels and the recorded trend
sections.html:
Among the small number of records reporting static water levels, the median depth to water is 40 feet below the surface. The middle half runs from 15 to 65 feet. That matters for pump selection, trenching, and estimating how much lift the system will need, but water levels can vary with season, location, and well use.

The decade figures do not show a recorded decline in this dataset. The median measured water level was 56 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 36 feet below the surface in the 2020s, meaning the later median was shallower. Only 27 wells report static water levels, so treat this as a limited record rather than a basin-wide conclusion.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Cedaredge, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity is spread across the decades, with the largest group issued in the 2000s at 260 permits. The records include 130 from the 1990s, 78 from the 1970s, 61 from the 2010s, 46 from the 1980s, 46 from the 2020s, and 11 from the 1960s. The newest permit year is 2025. Most permits are for domestic or household use at 75%; stock is 13%, irrigation is 6%, and monitoring is 9%.

The most active drillers in these records are Bill Kissner Drilling Inc (Kissner, Bill F.) with 158 wells, Wildcat Drilling & Pump, Inc. (Kissner, Billy D.) with 133, and K. W. Anderson Drilling (Anderson, Kermit W) with 40. Past work is useful local evidence, not a promise for a new site.

sections.heading: What a new Cedaredge well may cost
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground described in the local cost model, the typical drilling rate is $50-$75 per foot. At the 110-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $5,500-$8,200. That is only the drilling portion.

A finished system with the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $11,500-$20,200 at the median depth. A quote can move outside that range if the hole is deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the site needs more trenching and electrical work. Get the bid in writing and ask what happens if the driller must continue beyond the planned depth.

sections.heading: Cedaredge risks: water quality, dry holes, and the homesite
sections.html:
Mapped environmental information deserves a parcel-specific check. Within about 10 miles are 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 49 historic mine features, and 10 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped locations do not establish that a particular well is contaminated, but they are good reasons to review the well location, test existing water, and ask about nearby land uses.

Low yield is not the only concern. Confirm casing, grout, pump setting, and the well's permitted use. Check septic setbacks and the proposed building area before buying. An attractive homesite can become expensive if the driveway, septic system, well, and house cannot fit together. In an over-appropriated basin, an augmentation plan may also be required for some uses, so verify the permit conditions with Colorado DWR.

sections.heading: Buying or building near Cedaredge
sections.html:
Start with the neighboring wells, not just the listing description. Compare depths, reported yields, static water levels, aquifer descriptions, and uses for properties near the lot. Orchard City is about 6 miles away, while Delta and Hotchkiss are about 13 miles away; Lazear, Paonia, and Olathe provide additional nearby context, but the closest comparable wells are usually more useful than a broad regional average.

Before closing, obtain the permit and construction report, confirm the well location, and arrange water testing. For a new build, have the driller, septic designer, and excavation contractor review the site together. Carry a budget that allows for the local finished-system estimate and additional work if the actual depth, access, electrical run, or septic layout differs from the plan.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Cedaredge, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded well depth near Cedaredge is 110 feet. The middle half of reported depths runs from 71 to 167 feet, while the 90th percentile is 229 feet. Most wells are between 100 and 300 feet, but individual sites can differ because the local records are dominated by unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Cedaredge?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50-$75 per foot. At the 110-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $5,500-$8,200. A finished system including the pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $11,500-$20,200. A deeper hole or difficult access can increase the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do Cedaredge wells produce?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0-15.0 gallons per minute. Records show 59% producing more than 15 gallons per minute, while 9% produce between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. These are reported well results, not a guarantee for a new well on a specific lot.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Cedaredge?
faq.a: Permit records do not prove that water is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, the area has 17 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 49 historic mine features, and 10 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well water, especially before purchase, and review the well location and nearby land uses with a qualified professional.

faq.q: Are Cedaredge well water levels going down?
faq.a: The limited reported data does not show a dropping trend. The median static water level was 56 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 36 feet below the surface in the 2020s, which is shallower in the later period. Only 27 wells report static water levels, so this should not be treated as a complete groundwater assessment.
